A group of countries and partners, co-led by Colombia, Norway, and the UK, have translated the vision into 4 practical recommendations with concrete country examples. First, we need to consider data and statistics a public good. Most countries collect large volumes of data. Different agencies gather information for their own purposes, but do not share or publish them. The result is that much valuable information remains unused, and locked away, even when it could be crucial for decisions on tax, debt, spending, and service delivery. In South Africa, the National Treasury Secure Data Facility shows what a different approach looks like. By enabling controlled, de-identified access to linked tax microdata, it has unlocked research on corporate and personal income tax reforms, youth employment incentives, and multinational compliance. Fiscal policy that once relied on partial evidence is now informed by granular, nationally owned data under clear governance that protects confidentiality and public trust. Second, we must improve national data and statistical system coordination. Data and statistics are cutting across all sectors, from education to health and to financing. In many countries, each sector operates in silo with little interaction, or data sharing. To mitigate this, national coordination mechanisms need to be strengthened or established, and roles and priorities jointly defined. A range of actors, including governments, academia, civil society, and private sector, should be involved, and user needs should guide decisions. In Timor-Leste, the Ministry of Education brought together previously fragmented education data and presented a coherent evidence-based case to the Ministry of Finance during budget negotiations. The result was a significant increase in education funding and stronger inter-ministerial trust. The case shows that coordination across silos can turn existing data into a powerful tool for domestic resource allocation. Another point under this recommendation is that development partners need to align behind country-led data strategies rather than creating parallel projects specific systems. In doing so, it would also align with the International Development Corporation's severe commitments on reducing fragmentation. The third recommendation is to strengthen data governance and information innovation. Countries cannot run 21st century financing systems on 20th century data infrastructure. Today, many countries have differing legal frameworks, standards, and technical systems. To collaborate, it is key to put in place clear, consistent frameworks and shared standards, including strong provisions on privacy, confidentiality, and security, as well as ensuring that marginalized groups remain visible. Data also need to be set up in machine-readable formats to allow use of innovative tools like AI. An example from Somalia shows why governance and innovation matter in fragile contexts. With no recent census and limited access on the ground, the statistical office used satellite imagery and machine learning to identify and map internally displaced persons. Clear arrangements on ownership, methods, and data sharing meant the results could be trusted and reused by government and humanitarian actors to target assistance and plan services. Fourth, we must invest in national data and statistical capacity. The demand for data has substantially increased, but funding has remained fragmented. GDP is a clear example. It remains central in the FFD debate, including for debt sustainability analysis and access to finance. But investment in core economic data is a challenge. Without updated economic statistics, it's difficult to update the GDP base year. When the economy changes, the changes won't be captured, and economic sectors may be undervalued, or missed entirely. Overall, it is key that national governments increasingly invest in strengthening their own systems to deliver future efficiencies. Donors and partners should work alongside the government to prioritize national system strengthening rather than through parallel and extractive mechanisms. So, to conclude, we'd encourage all delegations to read our recommendations. Ask yourself, do you have the information you need to make the best use of your finance? Do you have a data system that can respond to emerging information needs? Thank you.

Finally, we appreciate the shout-out to the government and the people of Spain who invested heavily into hosting the conference and ensuring momentum for its follow-up with the launch of the Sevilla Platform for Action. There are also a few things that we would have liked to see. For one, it lacks explicit mention of the existential threat of the triple planetary crisis. There are also no references to inequalities, including gender inequality, and we would have liked to see language on human rights explicitly in the text, as we see this being an integral part of development. Likewise, initiatives such as the ongoing OECD DAC review TOSSD, or the Finance in Common Network could have been mentioned, as these are concrete examples of work that is progressing and can meaningfully contribute to implementation. in its current format, the paragraph appears to reflect a limited and selective framing approach, privileges a single narrative while other relevant realities and factual dimensions are not reflected. Mesdames les facilitateurs, facilitators, the delegation of Haiti. These problems and differences do not detract from the content of the amendment. They, on the contrary, strengthen the importance of it. Haiti recalls the need to respect international law in line with the International Charter, including the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity. In this spirit, Haiti joined the consensus on the amendment while underscoring that it must be interpreted in a balanced manner, in a non-politicized manner, and it must be adaptable to different situations where critical infrastructure is threatened. For Haiti, this approach must also open the way for enhanced international cooperation to help boost national capacities, to rebuild infrastructure, and to achieve resilience to shocks and access to financing for development. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President. Excellencies, colleagues, as we come to the close of this Forum, let me begin by thanking you. Thanking you for your candour, thanking you for staying focused on what is at stake, and thank you for your determination. This week has reminded us of something important that came out of Seville: that despite a challenging global environment, the world can still come together, can still find common ground, and can still find solutions to shared challenges. Let me leave you with 3 takeaways. First, the pressure on developing countries is intensifying. Across our discussions, we heard again and again that many countries are being asked to do more with less— less fiscal space, less room to absorb shocks, and less certainty in the global environment. And new pressures are compounding old ones. The conflict in the Middle East is sending economic shockwaves far beyond the region, through energy prices, food systems, inflation, exchange rate pressures, and higher borrowing costs. For countries already carrying heavy debt burdens and facing limited policy space, these are grave threats to their development progress. Second, our focus must pivot from commitments to delivery, and the pressure on developing countries makes that pivot increasingly urgent. Climate finance must flow at the scale needed to ensure energy security. Progress on international tax must advance so countries can mobilize resources and expand fiscal space, and investments in critical minerals must be managed to enable developing economies to claim a stake in the new economic opportunities rather than watch the value extracted and flow elsewhere. The Borrowers Platform launched last week is a positive example of words translating into actions, a practical instrument built to give countries navigating debt challenges somewhere to turn for advice grounded in their own experience. I look forward to watching it take shape. The severe commitment must now translate into progress that countries can see and feel— jobs created, infrastructure built, families protected, communities made resilient, opportunity within reach, not in theory but in practice. And third, none of this will happen at the scale that is required without stronger cooperation and stronger accountability. National leadership is indispensable. Country ownership is essential. And I'm pleased to see the National Focal Point Network that was launched this week. But countries cannot build resilience alone in a volatile and fragmented world. They need an international system that works for them, institutions that are responsive, to their needs, partnerships that are coherent, and follow-up that is credible. And that is why the discussions this week on coordination, on country-led strategies, and on data monitoring and follow-up are so important. Implementation does not advance through good intentions alone. It advances when partners work together, when incentives align, and when actors are held to account. Excellencies, the real test begins now. The success of Seville will not be judged by the commitments that were made last June, but by whether those commitments change financing conditions for the countries that need them most. Through our success, we can restore confidence that multilateralism can still deliver where it matters most. That is the responsibility before us. So let us leave the Forum with a sense of urgency with discipline and with a shared commitment to turn momentum into results, because financing for development is ultimately about building a more stable, more just, and a more hopeful future for everyone to live a life of dignity. I thank you.

Madam Deputy Secretary-General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, as we draw the 2026 ECOSOC Forum on Financing for Development follow-up to a close, I'm struck by the depth of the engagement and the strong spirit of cooperation that has characterized our discussions. Over the past days, our exchanges have reaffirmed that the financing for development process remains a central pillar of international cooperation at a time of profound global uncertainty and risk. Our discussions have underscored both the ambitions of that agreement as well as the urgency of its implementation. We have explored critical issues across the financing landscape, from mobilizing sustainable investment and addressing debt vulnerabilities to advancing reforms of the international financial architecture and strengthening data and accountability systems. We have also reflected on the importance of ensuring that our efforts are inclusive, they are country-led, and they are responsive to the needs of those most at risk of being left behind. Our richness of dialogue has highlighted not only the scale of the challenges before us, but also the growing momentum for action. The continued engagement of the member states and the stakeholders and the initiatives, including under the Sabia Platform of Actions, demonstrate that implementation is already underway. At the same time, it is also clear that much more must be done in order to close the financing gap, to reduce inequalities, and most importantly, to restore confidence in the multilateral systems. Excellencies, This Forum highlighted the importance of strengthening coherence across the international systems, including with the international financial institutions and other key partners. As we move forward, our collective focus must remain firmly on the implementation— that is, translating commitments into concrete actions at the national, at the regional, and at the global levels. The outcomes of this forum will contribute to guiding these efforts, including through the ongoing follow-up to the Sofia Commitment and the broader 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The challenges we face are significant, but so to each our shared determinations. Let us carry forward the momentum generated here and continue to work together in a spirit of solidarity and in a spirit of stronger partnerships. Let us remain steadfast in our commitment to a more inclusive, more resilient, and more sustainable global economy. And let us ensure that our collective efforts deliver meaningful progress for all.
